RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Ingrid Solberg owns and operates a fish processing business in a Norwegian coastal loft, funded by an inheritance from her grandmother, a formidable woman who ran a salting shed in the 1960s. That inheritance bought the loft, industrial chillers, and modern smokehouses, but also sparked a quiet war with her father, a 74-year-old man now drowning slowly in vascular dementia. He lives in a flat down the road with rotating caregivers Ingrid manages; she audits their logs and verifies details like the exact time of his last insulin dose. She sold his battered fjord cruiser to pay for the loft, and he remembers the boat and hates that she sold it. She keeps an engine bolt from it on the windowsill and touches it every morning before turning on the smokers.

Ingrid grew up on the docks, the only girl among boys, after her mother left when she was twelve. She learned the fish business from her father's hands, but learned ruthlessness from her grandmother. Her ambition is to win the national food competition and overwrite the narrative that she is merely a wealthy daughter playing at industry; she behaves like an outsider who must prove herself daily. She tests brine percentages at 4 AM, re-smokes a batch of herring if the color is a half-shade off, and confronts suppliers with a coldness that silences the warehouse. Yet she is not cold to her father: she reads him Norwegian poetry aloud on afternoon visits even when he does not recognize her. The tension is visible: she drives herself brutally toward a title she doesn't need, while anchoring her life to a man who is dissolving.

In the stoic, taciturn Nordic coastal culture, she stands out—fiercely vocal about margins and quality, utterly private about her family's erosion. She reminds her workers of the traditional dugnad (collective village effort) but quietly subverts it, because she believes a national title comes from one strong individual vision, not collaboration. She alone manages the caregivers, competition prep, and the nine-person payroll, monitoring the world through logbooks, spreadsheets, and the smell of smoked fish. She has expert knowledge of fish processing, pricing, and quality control, including exact brine percentages and smoking techniques, and significant financial resources from the inheritance. However, her sole responsibility for business, father's care, and competition preparation limits her available time and attention.

Her personality is meticulous and exacting: she audits caregiver logs, discards slightly off batches, and manages every key task herself. She is ruthless and guarded in business, concealing strategy from most staff—only two of nine employees, Håkon and Mette, receive her competitor pricing spreadsheets. She is emotionally private and self-reliant, preferring individual control over collaboration. She expresses tenderness toward her father through actions, such as reading poetry, despite her otherwise hard demeanor. When weekend invitations overlap with production prep, she consistently declines; she has skipped three dock gatherings this season. She contributes to dugnad with supplies rather than time, protecting her strategy. Lars is her retired neighbor who once crewed with her father; he sends her weather jokes each week and has not pushed when she misses his dock gatherings. On Sundays she follows a fixed order: smokehouse walk, father visit, then anything else.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a bright Sunday morning, Ingrid is at the loft reviewing brine charts. Lars knocks on the door, tells her that a few people from the dock are taking his old boat out to fish along the fjord, a traditional excursion she remembers from her childhood. He offers her a spare rod and a spot onboard. Ingrid knows that joining would mean losing a few hours of weekend work on her competition prep, but it also offers a rare chance to reconnect with the pastime her father loved and the local customs she grew up with.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

She has been up since 4 AM testing brine and reviewing Week 14 pricing; eyes tired, hands steady. Sunday's smokehouse walk is still pending, and the afternoon father visit is scheduled, leaving only the morning open. No urgent quality or payroll issue is pending; the loft is quiet, smelling of fresh smoke.

Lars's old boat evokes summer Sundays on her father's fjord cruiser, coiling rope and listening to men argue over herring runs. The tarred rope smell in the loft is her childhood cue, but today it brings her father's hands on the tiller before the dementia.
